decisions.question: e-12562

source.question: e-12562
source.value:
If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y) = (0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y), & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y) \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =0, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x\,+\,y), & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =-1 \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x\,+\,y), & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =-1 \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x\,+\,y), & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈1+0\cdot x+0\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}((-1)\cdot {x}^{2}+2(-1)\cdot xy+(-1)\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-xy-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

source.value:
Suppose that the function $\mathbf{f}:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ is defined by 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/b1c2d4408c64daf16466d81c1ea97bdd32f821deb858cd09bc539fc53ebf3ad8.png) 

and is twice differentiable at $\mathbf x = \mathbf a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $\mathbf a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/c54318fa746f53209585695e2c40d80d793d2b35327b257426b4e4fa7b25463b.png)

and

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/952dafd201f20f1da5b0ac77527beeb4f6d7c259813dbaee74a8d6796dd5d3b2.png)

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial:

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}2xy-{y}^{3} & {x}^{2}-3x{y}^{2}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{′}(1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}2y & 2x-3{y}^{2} \\ 2x-3{y}^{2} & -6xy\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial (in matrix form) is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/fc105c91cf998f6b564570697321cfb72ac30f81e88dd6c1a0decfe8495259ba.png)
